text: One minute to seven. The rooftop feast is ready, and the stool beside Seoa is still empty.
Her phone ticks over to seven.
The door bangs open, and Jaeha stumbles in holding up seven shaking fingers. Promise kept.
Seoa loses the fight not to smile. Technically, he's on time. Now sit.
Then the crew: Uncle Pyo with soju, Dami with her daughter, the brothers with chicken from a shop that doesn't exist yet.
The table goes quiet. Moon Ahin has arrived with a giant fruit basket. Jaeha admits he invited her. She'd rather they believed she was passing.
She perches on a plastic stool like it's a throne. More pets, asks the landlady. Nib has heard this before.
Seoa climbs onto her stool, cheeks red, and raises her cup. There's only one toast tonight.
Every cup goes up, plus a juice box and a lettuce leaf: to everyone who came back.
Jaeha picks up his chopsticks, and the tips won't meet.
He tells his fingers to close, like an order through Link. They don't answer.
Seoa's smile goes out.
He slides off the stool. Four people lunge for him. His body has gone critical.
Saturday, three a.m., a hospital ward. Seoa sleeps holding his hand. Nib watches from the windowsill.
Fourteen times past his limit, says the window. Body rating F. Once more, and it's his heart.
He reads it line by line, like a contract.
Then a small, cold smile. Every number in his life has gone up since Gate 0912. This one can too.
Nib comforts him his own way, reminding him who watched him fall off that stool.
By morning, the scans say he's perfectly healthy.
Seoa rounds on the doctor with the obvious question. He hides behind his tablet. Stress?
Yerin finds nothing to heal. No wound, just a body that's been used up.
The card is pure Moon Ahin: get well soon, and don't forget who got him through that rim.
Then Choi admits he knows someone. He describes her like a storm.
Everything Choi knows about rescue, she taught him, the hard way by the look of it.
So that night, the rescue van heads south, toward the coast.
Jaeha sleeps, hands still shaking. Lyra complains about this world's sizes. Borro, folded in half, is content.
Busan, Sunday at dawn. At the edge of the harbour market, an orange tent glows.
Inside, a short, broad old woman stirs a giant pan of tteokbokki, her left arm battered steel.
Choi announces himself, polite as a schoolboy. She doesn't turn round. He's alive, so he should eat.
She turns, ladle raised like a sword, gold tooth glinting. Geum Okran. Retired S-rank. The Wall of Busan.
She comes round the counter, already knowing about the chopsticks. Even Borro steps back.
She taps him with the ladle like a doctor's hammer, joint by joint. Every one has carried too much.
Then she presses it over his heart. That's where all of it landed.
Then one light tap on the forehead. That part, she allows, still works.
And then the verdict. Your head is S-rank. Your body is garbage.
Nib nods. Lyra nods. Even Borro nods. Choi hides a laugh behind his coffee.
Then she drops her voice. She knows what he does, and roughly how often. Once more, his heart stops.
He has the exact count: fourteen. Then it hits him. He never told her about Carry.
She looks out at the sea, steel fingers flexing. She's seen it once before: ten years ago, the night of the Opening.
Jaeha's eyes go wide. The night he and Seoa lost their parents.
Before he can ask, the ladle is in his face: food, training, then questions.
Her steel hand wraps his shaking fingers round a hot cup of tteokbokki.
She lets go. The sauce sloshes, but he holds on. That's set one.
Lyra asks whether this is training or torture. Auntie Geum doesn't see the difference.
Her timetable starts before dawn, breaks for tteokbokki, and never really ends.
Its last line is her favourite: one more set, then just one more.
Choi whispers his expert opinion: she likes him. His evidence: Jaeha's head is still unbonked.
Without turning round, she flicks the ladle back and bonks Choi on the head.
And Jaeha laughs for the first time in days, without dropping the cup.
The system makes it official: a new quest, named after her. The reward is question marks.
He accepts with a trembling finger. Of course he does.
For one moment, his fingers close tighter round the cup, and the shaking eases.
He looks at his steadier hands, then at her back. Naturally, he wants more.
A slow, gold-toothed grin. He's been doing set two all along. The cup is still in his hands.
The sun comes up over the harbour, Borro's mossy back sticking out of the tent.
Auntie Geum steps out and stops. The Wall of Busan doesn't like her sea today.
Her steel fingers clench and unclench, all by themselves.
Out on the water, everything is calm. Nothing wrong at all.
Below the surface, the light turns gold, then blue, then dark.
On the seabed lies a ring of gate light three hundred metres wide, under old stone and ten-year-old steel.
One old steel plate shears its bolts, and violet light bubbles up through the crack.
And under the lid, something enormous slides past in the dark.
In the tent, Jaeha's head snaps up. A sealed gate is failing, close by. Nib turns to the sea.
Auntie Geum stands beside him, eyes on the calm sea. The cup is steady now. Drink up, kid. He'll need that body.
High over Busan, the harbour shines, and far out, a violet stain spreads across the calm sea. His summons will go first. This time, his body has to keep up.
